(CNN)  -- Is the movie cop thriller heading for retirement? Colin Farrell, left, and Edward Norton star in "Pride and Glory" as New York cops. It seems incredible to suggest that such a popular form of storytelling might be on the way out, but it's happened before: Musicals and westerns were once staple entertainment for the moviegoing masses, and somewhere in the 1970s they just went thataway. Now the musicals and westerns that emerge are considered unusual. So consider: Last week the top box-office draw in the country was "Max Payne" with Mark Wahlberg as an obsessed cop tracking down the killer who murdered his wife and child. Based on a video game, "Max Payne" takes a rudimentary plot and boils it down still further, to the point where it's worse than predictable. The film's attraction (such as it is) isn't found in story, but in decoration: the blue-filtered chiaroscuro and etch-y comic book compositions, how the snow glints under the streetlights. "Pride and Glory," on the other hand, is resolutely old school. Not only is it not based on a video game, it's hard to imagine that any of the characters has played one -- or seen a movie either.  Watch behind the scenes at "Pride and Glory" » . The time period isn't specified, but it seems to be today, going on 1974. Written by "Tumbleweeds" director Gavin O'Connor and Joe Carnahan ("Narc"), based on a story O'Connor put together with his twin brother Greg and ex-New York cop Robert Hopes, this is one of those movies that wants to emulate the serious side of '70s cinema, to dig into thorny ethical quandaries and alert us to institutional corruption. Unfortunately, it does a poor job. This time Edward Norton is the alienated cop, Ray Tierney. Like Max Payne, he's stepped away from the street to nurse his own grievances -- he bears an ugly scar down his cheek from an incident referred to only obliquely. The details remain hazy, but it casts a "Chinatown"-size cloud over Ray and probably accounts for the state of his marriage -- which is over -- and the fact that he's sleeping on his dad's leaky sailboat. There's considerably more plot in "Pride and Glory" than in "Max Payne," but it's only marginally less predictable. A shooting puts four cops down -- all of them from the command of Ray's brother Francis (Noah Emmerich). Francis is devastated, and the boys' father, Francis Sr. (Jon Voight), insists Ray must step up and take charge of the investigation. The Tierney clan has another cop in the family: Jimmy (Colin Farrell) is married to their sister (Lake Bell). We soon realize Jimmy's hands are dirty. But what will Ray do about it? If you've seen your Sidney Lumet movies -- "Serpico," "Prince of the City," "Q&A" -- then you'll be well ahead of the game. Even if you haven't, you'll have seen the cop shows that drew from them. Which is why almost every scene, every line of dialogue in "Pride and Glory" has the dull thud of cliche. "We can't keep doing this," moans Ray's soon-to-be ex-wife. Any regular moviegoer will know exactly what she means: How many more times will we have to suffer this déja-vu? Granted, originality isn't everything. Last year, James Grey's "We Own the Night" invested a very similar story with subtle character shadings and a subversive edge. What's most disappointing about O'Connor's capably acted but gloomy and portentous movie is how it shies away from any real complexity. The Tierneys may have their faults, but the outsider, Jimmy, is the bad egg (we gather that much when he threatens a baby with a hot iron). When push comes to shove, the brothers do the right thing in a climax so stock you could use it to make gravy. The old school was better than this. And, back then, it wasn't old either. ***

**(CNN)** — Is the cinematic police thriller facing extinction? 

Colin Farrell (left) and Edward Norton star as New York police officers in *Pride and Glory*. Suggesting that such a enduringly popular genre might be on the decline feels counterintuitive, yet history demonstrates that it is entirely possible. Musicals and Westerns were once the bedrock of mainstream cinematic entertainment, only to quietly fade from dominance during the 1970s. Today, new entries in those genres are treated as rare anomalies.

Consider the current box-office landscape: last week’s top-grossing film was *Max Payne*, starring Mark Wahlberg as an obsessed detective hunting the killer of his wife and child. Adapted from a video game, *Max Payne* strips a rudimentary plot down to its absolute barest elements, rendering it far worse than merely predictable. The film’s appeal—such as it is—lies not in narrative substance, but in stylistic embellishment: blue-filtered chiaroscuro, stylized comic-book compositions, and the glint of streetlights on falling snow.

*Pride and Glory*, by contrast, is resolutely old-school. Far from being derived from a video game, it is difficult to imagine any of its characters having ever played one—or even watched a movie, for that matter. 

[Watch behind the scenes at *Pride and Glory* »]

Though nominally set in the present day, the film feels perpetually stuck in 1974. Directed by Gavin O’Connor (*Tumbleweeds*) and co-written with Joe Carnahan (*Narc*)—from a story O'Connor developed alongside his twin brother, Greg, and former NYPD officer Robert Hopes—it attempts to evoke the serious, atmospheric cinema of the 1970s. It aspires to grapple with complex ethical dilemmas and expose systemic corruption; regrettably, it falls well short of those ambitions.

This time, Edward Norton portrays the alienated detective, Ray Tierney. Much like Max Payne, Ray has retreated from active duty to nurse his personal grievances, bearing a severe facial scar from a past incident referenced only obliquely. Though the details remain hazy, this lingering trauma casts a *Chinatown*-esque shadow over Ray, accounting for his failed marriage and his current residence aboard his father’s leaky sailboat.

While *Pride and Glory* offers considerably more plot than *Max Payne*, it proves only marginally less predictable. A fatal shooting leaves four officers dead—all serving under the command of Ray’s brother, Francis (Noah Emmerich). Devastated by the tragedy, their father, Francis Sr. (Jon Voight), insists that Ray step up to lead the investigation. The Tierney law-enforcement dynasty includes yet another officer: Jimmy (Colin Farrell), who is married to the brothers' sister (Lake Bell). It soon becomes evident that Jimmy is deeply corrupt, posing a crucial dilemma: how will Ray respond?

Audiences familiar with the classic filmography of Sidney Lumet—such as *Serpico*, *Prince of the City*, and *Q&A*—will easily anticipate every narrative turn. Even those unacquainted with Lumet’s work will recognize the tropes, which have been endlessly recycled in modern television procedurals. Consequently, nearly every scene and line of dialogue in *Pride and Glory* lands with the dull thud of cliché. "We can't keep doing this," laments Ray's estranged wife. Any seasoned moviegoer will know precisely how she feels, wondering how many more times we must endure this sense of cinematic déjà-vu.

To be fair, absolute originality is not a strict prerequisite. Last year, James Gray’s *We Own the Night* infused a remarkably similar premise with subtle character nuances and a sharp, subversive edge. What makes O’Connor’s capably acted yet gloomy and portentous film so disappointing is its reluctance to engage with genuine moral complexity. While the Tierneys are not without their flaws, the narrative conveniently concentrates its bad behavior on Jimmy, the family outsider (a point heavy-handedly established when he threatens an infant with a hot iron). When the climax arrives, the brothers inevitably do the right thing in a resolution so stock it feels prefabricated. 

The classic cinema *Pride and Glory* seeks to honor was far superior—and in its heyday, it was anything but old.

***Pride and Glory* is rated R and has a running time of 129 minutes.**

***

### The Twilight of the Cop Thriller

Cinematic history is defined by the rise and fall of its dominant genres. Just as the Western once ruled the American box office before fading into a niche nostalgia, and the classic Hollywood musical gave way to changing cultural tastes, the traditional cop thriller now appears to be entering its own period of decline. Once a mainstay of popular cinema, the genre increasingly struggles to find fresh narrative ground. Modern entries in the genre often illustrate this struggle, attempting to revitalize tired tropes through either radical stylistic choices or heavy-handed nostalgia, yet frequently failing to capture the magic of their predecessors.

At the heart of this contemporary genre fatigue is a shared character archetype: the broken, alienated law enforcer. Recent additions to the genre, such as *Max Payne* and *Pride and Glory*, both center on protagonists who have retreated from standard duty to cope with profound personal trauma. These leads are no longer the righteous, clear-headed crusaders of early cinema; instead, they are disillusioned figures operating on the fringes of the very systems they once represented. This pervasive sense of psychological isolation mirrors the larger exhaustion of the genre itself, suggesting a fundamental uncertainty about what a police hero should look like in the modern era.

To compensate for a dwindling narrative landscape, filmmakers have taken starkly different approaches to keeping the cop thriller relevant. In *Max Payne*, the film abandons traditional storytelling rigor in favor of pure visual spectacle. Adapting the video game property, the movie relies heavily on hyper-stylized aesthetics, neo-noir atmospheres, and comic-book visual effects. However, by prioritizing slick graphics and surreal imagery over a well-developed storyline, *Max Payne* ultimately becomes a clear example of style over substance, offering visual flair at the expense of emotional and dramatic engagement.

Conversely, *Pride and Glory* takes an earnest, retro approach by attempting to emulate the gritty, morally complex cinema of the 1970s. The film sets out to tackle serious themes, diving deep into institutional corruption, familial loyalty, and complex ethical dilemmas reminiscent of classics like *Serpico* or *The Godfather*. Yet, despite its ambitious desire to revisit the weight and realism of classic crime dramas, *Pride and Glory* falls short. The film suffers from a clunky narrative execution, failing to deliver the nuanced storytelling required to make its grand dramatic ambitions land with genuine impact.

Ultimately, both *Max Payne* and *Pride and Glory* demonstrate the dilemma currently facing the cop thriller. Whether attempting to reinvent itself through modern, hyper-stylized visual aesthetics or looking backward to the dark, ethical complexity of 1970s cinema, the genre is struggling to execute a meaningful vision. As these divergent paths show, without strong narrative foundations, the traditional police drama may well be following the Western toward cinematic history.

The Western, which once dominated the box office, eventually retreated into nostalgic myth, while the classic movie musical faded as audience sensibilities shifted away from grand theatricality. Today, a similar question hangs over contemporary cinema: Is the police thriller facing its own slow extinction? For decades, the cop movie served as a reliable staple of American film, capturing public anxiety around urban decay, institutional corruption, and the thin line between law and lawlessness. Yet, an examination of recent releases suggests the genre has reached a critical impasse, suffering from a profound creative exhaustion.

This stagnation is clearly visible in the stark divide between two recent entries in the genre, which approach the material from opposite ends of the stylistic spectrum. On one extreme sits *Max Payne*, a film heavily reliant on the logic and aesthetics of its video game source material. *Max Payne* prioritizes visual spectacle above all else, drowning the audience in a sea of heavily stylized neo-noir imagery, digital effects, and slow-motion gunfights. Yet, beneath its glossy, rain-slicked surface lies a thoroughly hollow core. The narrative is utterly predictable, the dialogue is derivative, and the central detective is reduced to a flat avatar moving through a digital landscape. By prioritizing superficial style over character development and genuine tension, the film demonstrates how the cop thriller can be diluted into empty visual noise.

On the other end of the spectrum sits *Pride and Glory*, a film that deliberately rejects digital hyper-realism in favor of a traditional, character-driven approach. Explicitly evoking the gritty, morally complex police dramas of the 1970s—such as *Serpico* or *The French Connection*—the film attempts a serious institutional critique. Centering on a family of NYPD officers torn apart by systemic corruption and misplaced loyalty, *Pride and Glory* promises a hard-hitting look at the moral compromises of law enforcement. However, despite its earnest intentions and prestige cast, the movie ultimately falters. Its critique of corruption feels recycled rather than incisive, collapsing under the weight of tired tropes, melodramatic family dynamics, and a heavy-handed narrative that offers nothing new to the conversation.

Together, these two films illustrate the existential trap in which the modern cop thriller finds itself. Filmmakers seem caught between two uninspired choices: treating the genre as a shallow, video-game-inspired stunt show, or recycling decades-old formulas in a failed attempt to capture a bygone era of gritty realism. Neither approach yields a vital, resonant film. When a genre is reduced to either empty visual gymnastics or unconvincing, nostalgic posturing, it loses its ability to engage meaningfully with real-world complexities.

Much like the Western before it, the traditional cop thriller appears to have exhausted its central mythology. The simple binaries of good cops versus bad cops, or noble rogues fighting corrupt systems, no longer hold the dramatic currency they once did. Unless filmmakers can break free from predictable plot lines and surface-level stylization to find a fresh, relevant perspective on power and justice, the cop thriller may soon take its place alongside the Western and the musical—a once-mighty cinematic staple reduced to a relic of Hollywood's past.

**Title:** From Hollywood Renaissance to Heartfelt Advocacy: Colin Farrell’s Moving Moment on CNN

Over the past two decades, Colin Farrell has undergone one of the most compelling transformations in modern cinema. Once known as Hollywood’s quintessential "bad boy" of the early 2000s, the Irish actor has evolved into an Oscar-nominated powerhouse, celebrated for his nuanced performances in films like *The Banshees of Inisherin* and his transformative role as Oz Cobb in *The Penguin*. However, in a recent candid interview on CNN, Farrell proved that his most impactful work is happening off-screen.

Sitting down with CNN anchors, Colin Farrell shifted the spotlight away from the glitz of movie premieres to discuss a deeply personal mission: the launch of the Colin Farrell Foundation. Created in honor of his eldest son, James, who lives with a rare neuro-genetic disorder called Angelman syndrome, the foundation aims to provide support, advocacy, and community programs for adult children with intellectual disabilities.

During the CNN segment, Farrell spoke with a level of vulnerability rarely seen among Hollywood A-listers. He highlighted a critical, often-overlooked issue that families face: the "cliff" that occurs when special-needs children turn 21 and lose access to many state-funded support systems. 

"Once your child turns 21, they’re kind of on their own," Farrell explained during the CNN interview, his voice heavy with empathy for families who lack the financial resources he possesses. "This is my way of using the platform I’ve been given to shine a light on a community that deserves dignity, support, and joy."

The CNN feature struck a chord with viewers worldwide, drawing praise for how openly Farrell discussed the joys and challenges of raising a child with special needs. It wasn't merely a press junket for a movie star; it was a powerful piece of advocacy that leveraged CNN's global reach to jumpstart an international conversation about disability care.

For Colin Farrell, appearing on platforms like CNN serves a dual purpose. While his acting career continues to thrive at an all-time high, his public discourse has shifted toward purpose-driven storytelling. By pairing his Hollywood prominence with genuine humanitarian efforts, Farrell is redefining what it means to be a leading man in the modern era—showing that true influence is measured not by box-office numbers, but by the lives we touch.

counterfactuals.output:
**Review: 'Pride and Glory' trades in familiar cop-drama tropes, saved only by its powerhouse cast**

**By** Tom Brueggemann *for CNN*
*(Archival Review — October 2008)*

**(CNN) —** In the cinematic ecosystem of New York City police dramas, Gavin O’Connor’s *Pride and Glory* arrives carrying a heavy inheritance. Coming in the long shadow of genre high-water marks like *Serpico*, *Prince of the City*, and more recently, Martin Scorsese’s Oscar-sweeping *The Departed*, this gritty procedural attempts to examine the toxic intersection of family loyalty and institutional corruption. 

While it packs an undisputed emotional wallop—thanks largely to ferocious performances from stars Edward Norton and Colin Farrell—*Pride and Glory* ultimately feels weighed down by the very clichés it tries so earnestly to unpack.

### A Family Affair on the Fringes of Manhattan

The film opens with a horrific jolt: four NYPD officers are ambushed and killed in a Washington Heights apartment during a drug bust gone bad. The tragedy strikes at the heart of the Tierneys, a multi-generational Irish-American law enforcement dynasty. 

At the top sits the booze-weathered patriarch, Assistant Chief Francis Tierney Sr. (Jon Voight), who commands his missing-in-action son, Ray (Edward Norton), to lead the task force investigating the murders. Ray, a detective sidelined by a past scandal that left his conscience battered, reluctantly accepts. 

The case immediately drags Ray into the orbit of his own family: his older brother, Francis Jr. (Noah Emmerich), is the precinct’s embattled commander, while his charismatic, hot-headed brother-in-law, Jimmy Egan (Colin Farrell), is a street-level officer whose terrifyingly loose relationship with the law becomes the central focus of the investigation. 

It quickly becomes clear that the four dead cops weren't just victims of a street gang—they were casualties of a high-stakes, dirty-cop extortion ring operated right under the precinct's nose.

### Norton Broods, Farrell Explodes

If *Pride and Glory* works, it is because of the sheer force of its acting. 

Edward Norton turns in a characteristically soulful performance as Ray. Playing a man trapped between his moral compass and his love for his family, Norton uses his quiet, wounded eyes to convey a level of internal agony that the script doesn't always provide. He is the film’s moral center, but he plays it with a tired, bruised resignation rather than heroic bravado.

Opposite him, Colin Farrell is a lightning rod of toxic masculinity and unhinged charisma. As Jimmy Egan, Farrell gives one of his most intense, visceral performances of the late 2000s. Whether he is threatening a suspect with an iron or posturing at a family dinner, Farrell plays Jimmy not as a cartoon villain, but as a man who genuinely believes his illegal side-hustles are justified to provide for his family and protect his fellow officers. 

The scenes where Norton and Farrell go head-to-head carry a crackling tension. The contrast between Norton’s quiet integrity and Farrell’s volatile desperation provides the film with its best moments. 

Supporting turns from Noah Emmerich—as a weak man crumbling under the weight of his own turned-a-blind-eye negligence—and Jon Voight add necessary texture to the film’s central theme: the destructive nature of the "thin blue line" when it becomes a family bloodline.

### Heavy-Handed Melodrama

Where director Gavin O’Connor (*Miracle*) and co-writer Joe Carnahan (*Narc*) stumble is in their insistence on subtlety-free storytelling. 

*Pride and Glory* hits every beat you expect a 1970s-style cop thriller to hit: rain-slicked New York streets, smoky bars filled with bagpipes and slurred oaths of brotherhood, screaming arguments over dinner tables, and a climax that devolves into an improbable, physical showdown on a crowded street.

The film's tone is oppressive, almost aggressively bleak. While realism is clearly the goal—O'Connor shoots in real locations with a muted color palette—the narrative relies on heavy melodrama that feels increasingly manufactured as the film progresses. We’ve seen these compromised cops, these long-suffering wives, and these stoic brothers before, and often in better films or episodic television like HBO’s *The Wire*.

Furthermore, the film was famously delayed in its release by two years, and it shows. Arriving in late 2008, its story of institutional cover-ups feels a bit dated, lacking the sharp geopolitical or systemic commentary that modern audiences have come to expect from crime procedurals.

### The Verdict

*Pride and Glory* is a classic case of an elite cast elevating mid-tier material. It is a muscular, intensely acted drama that will satisfy fans of gritty police procedurals who don't mind a heavy dose of formula. But for those looking for a fresh take on the classic "good cop, bad cop" dynamic, O’Connor’s film offers plenty of pride, plenty of grief, but ultimately, very little new glory.

**CNN Rating:** ★★½ out of ★★★★ 
*(Rated R for pervasive language, strong violence, and brief drug content)*

# Is the cop thriller dying? What 'Max Payne' and 'Pride and Glory' tell us about a fading genre

**By David Miller, CNN**
Updated 11:42 AM EDT, Friday, October 24, 2008

---

### AT A GLANCE

**"Max Payne"** 
* **Runtime:** 100 minutes
* **MPAA Rating:** PG-13 (for violence including intense sequences of gunplay, drug content, sexuality, and language)
* **Director:** John Moore
* **Starring:** Mark Wahlberg, Mila Kunis, Beau Bridges

**"Pride and Glory"**
* **Runtime:** 130 minutes
* **MPAA Rating:** R (for strong violence, pervasive language, and brief drug use)
* **Director:** Gavin O'Connor
* **Starring:** Edward Norton, Colin Farrell, Jon Voight

---

**(CNN)** — In the late 1970s, Hollywood watched two of its most reliable cash cows bleed out at the box office. The Western, which had dominated screens for half a century, was suddenly deemed an artifact of a bygone era. The grand Hollywood musical, bloated and out of touch, met a similar fate. Audiences simply stopped believing in them. 

As we look at the marquee this month, a disturbing sense of déjà vu sets in. Is the urban cop thriller headed for the same cinematic graveyard?

Two major releases this October suggest the badge is severely losing its luster. On one end of the spectrum is John Moore’s *"Max Payne,"* a sleek, CGI-drenched video game adaptation. On the other is Gavin O’Connor’s *"Pride and Glory,"* a gritty, tear-stained family drama about NYPD corruption. Though wildly different in style, both films suffer from the same fatal diagnosis: acute narrative exhaustion.

```
       "Like the cowboy riding into the sunset in 1975, 
        the tormented detective on rain-slicked streets 
        may be running out of road."
```

### High style, low substance vs. heavy-handed melodrama

*"Max Payne"* attempts to breathe life into the genre by coating it in icy nord-noir aesthetics and supernatural imagery. Mark Wahlberg plays the titular DEA agent, frozen in grief over his murdered family. Yet beneath its slow-motion gunfights and snow-dusted, shadowy alleys, the film is an empty shell. It relies on stylized violence to mask a complete lack of human interest. It isn't a film about policing or justice; it’s an interactive shooter stripped of its controller.

Meanwhile, *"Pride and Glory"* takes itself intensely seriously. Boasting a powerhouse cast featuring Edward Norton, Colin Farrell, and Jon Voight, O’Connor’s film tries to be a sprawling tragedy about a multi-generational Irish-American cop family torn apart by moral rot. 

Farrell sneers, Norton broods, and Voight drinks heavily—yet we feel nothing. Why? Because we have seen this exact movie a dozen times before. *"Pride and Glory"* relies so heavily on worn-out clichés that you can check them off on a clip board: 
* The tormented detective who left the force after a traumatic incident (check).
* The charismatic brother-in-law who is secretly running a rogue strike team (check).
* The wise, booze-soaked patriarch trying to keep the "family honor" intact (check).
* The rain-slicked confrontation where bad guys wear leather jackets and smoke cigarettes under streetlights (check).

When a genre reduces its characters to archetypes and its plots to Mad Libs of blue-suited corruption, audience apathy is the inevitable result. 

### The ghost of Sidney Lumet

To understand how far the cop movie has fallen, one only needs to look back at the gold standard: the work of Sidney Lumet. 

In masterpieces like *"Serpico"* (1973) and *"Prince of the City"* (1981), Lumet didn't just give us bad cops and good cops trading gunfire. He examined the systemic weight of institutions. He understood that the tragedy of police corruption wasn't about a few "bad apples" or comic-book villains, but about how morally compromised systems force decent human beings into impossible corners. Lumet’s films were grounded in a terrifying, claustrophobic reality.

Today’s filmmakers seem to have forgotten Lumet's lessons. *"Pride and Glory"* mimics the surface texture of a Lumet film—the grey New York skies, the thick accents, the moral fatigue—but it trades true psychological depth for soap-opera melodrama. *"Max Payne"* abandons reality altogether, transforming police work into a superhero origin story.

### Is the badge beyond repair?

Genre deaths are rarely sudden; they are long, agonizing declines marked by creative repetition. Just as the Western sank under the weight of its own romantic myth-making, the cop thriller is choking on its own cynicism and tired tropes. 

This isn't to say the genre can never be saved. Just as Clint Eastwood resurrected the Western with *"Unforgiven"* in 1992, the cop film may one day find a director capable of stripping away the cliches and discovering something raw and truthful beneath the dark coat and the shiny shield.

For now, however, films like *"Max Payne"* and *"Pride and Glory"* offer little hope. They suggest that the movie cop—once the ultimate American antihero—has finally run out of cases to solve. 

**VERDICTS:** 
* *"Max Payne"*: **C-**
* *"Pride and Glory"*: **C**

counterfactuals.output:
**CNN.com** / SHOWBIZ / MOVIES  
**Byline:** CNN Film Critic  
**Date:** October 24, 2008  

---

### Review: 'Pride and Glory' trades 1970s nuance for modern noise

**(CNN)** — In a month where real-world chaos dominates the headlines—between Wall Street’s dizzying tailspin and an increasingly tense presidential race—you might expect moviegoers to seek a different kind of reality at the multiplex. Specifically, the dark, complex morality tales that American cinema used to excel at during times of national anxiety. 

Instead, this weekend brings us *Pride and Glory*, a gritty New York cop drama that wants desperately to be a modern-day classic, but ultimately proves how far Hollywood has fallen from the golden age of the police thriller. 

Directed by Gavin O’Connor, *Pride and Glory* lands in theaters surrounded by high expectations. Boasting an elite cast led by Edward Norton and Colin Farrell, and co-written by Joe Carnahan (*Narc*), the film dives headfirst into the dirty underbelly of the NYPD. The story centers on the Tierneys, a multi-generational Irish-American family of bravest and finest: Jon Voight plays the liquor-soaked patriarch, Noah Emmerich the high-ranking officer in charge of a troubled precinct, Norton the righteous detective dragged into an investigation, and Farrell his hot-headed brother-in-law who happens to be leading a ring of dirty cops.

On paper, it has all the ingredients of a masterpiece. On screen, it mostly feels like a collection of recycled tropes, dialed up to a punishing volume.

To understand why *Pride and Glory* feels so underwhelming, one only has to look back to the 1970s and early ’80s, when directors like Sidney Lumet transformed the police procedural into an art form. 

In Lumet’s *Serpico* (1973), Al Pacino’s Frank Serpico wasn't a heroic archetype fighting a few clear-cut "bad apples"; he was an eccentric, isolated man slowly suffocated by a sprawling, institutionalized system of quiet payoffs. The terror of *Serpico* wasn't in violent shootouts—it was in the cafeteria glares and the slow realization that doing the right thing made you an enemy of the state. 

Even more devastating was Lumet’s 1981 masterpiece *Prince of the City*, starring Treat Williams as Danny Ciello. That film understood that corruption isn't just a matter of evil men doing evil things; it’s an intricate, sticky web where loyalty to your brothers directly conflicts with loyalty to the law. *Prince of the City* took its time—nearly three hours—to show the agonizing psychological toll of betraying your own. It refused to give the audience easy answers or clean resolutions.

*Pride and Glory*, by contrast, mistakes intensity for depth. 

Where Lumet offered gray zones, O'Connor offers high-decibel melodrama. Farrell’s character, Jimmy Egan, isn’t allowed to be a tragic product of a broken system; he is practically written as a cartoon villain, threatening infants with hot irons to prove his menacing credentials. Norton’s Ray Tierney is so saintly and tortured that he feels less like a real NYPD detective and more like a cinematic martyr. 

The film relies heavily on modern cinematic shorthand for "grit"—shaky camera work, washed-out color palettes, and a relentless barrage of profanity—hoping it will pass for authenticity. But true grit doesn't come from a lens filter or a brutal interrogation scene; it comes from character nuance and systemic critique. 

We saw a flash of that true complexity earlier this decade with *The Wire* on television, or even Antoine Fuqua’s *Training Day* back in 2001, which at least gave Denzel Washington a magnetic, philosophical edge. But recent big-screen efforts—including last week’s CGI-drenched video game adaptation *Max Payne* and now *Pride and Glory*—suggest that Hollywood has forgotten how to write a simple, character-driven cop story. 

Instead of asking hard questions about power, institution, and morality, modern police thrillers prefer a simple narrative: bad guys take bribes, good guys punch them, and the badge is restored through bloodshed. 

*Pride and Glory* isn't a terrible movie; the performances, particularly from Norton and Emmerich, are far better than the script deserves. But in an era where Americans are grappling with systemic failures in real time, our movies ought to offer something more than slick, formulaic cynicism. 

If you're looking for a dark, compelling night at the movies this weekend, skip the box office line, head to the video rental store, and put on *Serpico* or *Prince of the City* instead. You'll find a lot more truth in those thirty-year-old shadows than in anything hitting the big screen today.

**CNN Rating:** **C+** *(Rated R for pervasive language, violence, and brief nudity)*

counterfactuals.output:
With its dark alleyways, bruised knuckles, and tortured moral dilemmas, the police drama has been a bedrock of American cinema for decades. But as *Pride and Glory* opens in theaters, industry observers are asking whether audiences have grown weary of the bad-cop, dirty-street formula.

Directed by Gavin O'Connor, *Pride and Glory* arrives packed with the genre's standard hallmarks. Edward Norton plays Ray Tierney, an honest, reluctant detective tasked with investigating a brutal precinct ambush that left four officers dead. Colin Farrell stars as Jimmy Egan, Ray’s charismatic brother-in-law, whose hands—and badge—might not be so clean. Add Jon Voight as the family's heavy-drinking police patriarch, and the film serves up a traditional recipe of blood loyalty versus legal duty.

It is a blueprint that used to print money and win awards. From 1970s classics like *The French Connection* and *Serpico* to modern hits like *L.A. Confidential* and *Training Day*, the urban cop thriller was long considered a guaranteed draw for adult audiences. Just two years ago, Martin Scorsese finally won his long-overdue Best Director Oscar with the Boston-based police drama *The Departed*.

Yet, the cinematic landscape is shifting rapidly.

Part of the challenge facing modern cop movies comes from the small screen. Groundbreaking television series such as HBO’s *The Wire* and FX’s *The Shield* spent much of the past decade dismantling traditional hero-and-villain tropes, offering intricate, long-form realism that a two-hour feature film struggles to match. When home viewers can watch critically acclaimed, complex police sagas on cable every week, convincing them to buy a movie ticket for similar terrain becomes a tough sell.

At the same time, Hollywood’s financial model has evolved. The mid-budget, R-rated drama intended for adult filmgoers is increasingly being squeezed out by broad PG-13 superhero franchises and visual-effects spectacles. 

"The cop movie isn't dead, but the cookie-cutter cop movie certainly is," says box office analyst Paul Dergarabedian. "Audiences still respond to a great morality play, but they won't pay for the same gritty-street tropes unless there's a truly fresh angle or an undeniable event factor."

*Pride and Glory* itself faced a long, troubled road to the screen, suffering years of production delays and release date postponements—a sign of studio anxiety over how to market a traditional, hard-boiled crime drama in today's marketplace.

For stars like Norton and Farrell, the film represents a passionate throwback to the character-driven cinema of the 1970s. But as opening-weekend numbers roll in, the box office performance of *Pride and Glory* may offer the ultimate verdict on whether moviegoers are still willing to follow a line of duty down those rain-soaked street corners, or if the classic cop thriller is finally ready to turn in its badge.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a comparative review of "Max Payne" and "Pride and Glory," highlighting why modern Hollywood struggles to innovate within the corrupt cop genre.
counterfactuals.output:
In the autumn of 2008, two films arrived in theaters representing opposite ends of the same genre spectrum: Gavin O’Connor’s *Pride and Glory*, a gritty, traditional New York police drama, and John Moore’s *Max Payne*, a heavily stylized, supernatural-leaning adaptation of a famous video game. Both films centered on the same foundational narrative engine—a lone, uncompromised detective uncovering deep-seated corruption within his own department. 

Both films were critical and narrative failures, albeit for entirely different reasons. Taken together, *Max Payne* and *Pride and Glory* serve as a perfect case study for why modern Hollywood consistently struggles to innovate within the corrupt cop genre. 

---

### *Pride and Glory*: Drowning in the Swamp of Cliché

*Pride and Glory* approaches the corrupt cop genre through the lens of tragic realism and generational duty. It stars Edward Norton as Ray Tierney, an honest detective tasked with investigating a violent precinct ambush that left four officers dead. The precinct is commanded by his brother Francis (Noah Emmerich), and the prime suspect’s unit includes his brother-in-law, Jimmy Egan (Colin Farrell). Ray quickly discovers that the dead officers were on the payroll of a rogue ring led by Jimmy, forcing a choice between the "Blue Wall of Silence" and abstract justice.

#### The Good
The film boasts an elite ensemble. Norton brings his signature intellectual weariness to the role, while Farrell leans aggressively into a volatile, charismatic darkness. The film captures the suffocating, cold ambience of wintertime New York, and director Gavin O’Connor understands the rhythmic, insular language of law enforcement families.

#### Where It Fails
*Pride and Glory* is entirely trapped by its own genre heritage. It attempts to walk in the footsteps of Sidney Lumet classics (*Serpico*, *Prince of the City*) and James Gray’s *The Yards*, but it lacks their subtlety. To establish Colin Farrell’s character as "corrupt," the screenplay abandons nuance and has him threaten a newborn baby with a hot iron. By reducing systemic police corruption to cartoonish, sociopathic cruelty, the film robs itself of any real moral ambiguity. It is a relentless, dreary march through every trope imaginable: the alcoholic patriarch father (Jon Voight), the wife dying of cancer, the rain-slicked alleyway beatings, and a climax that devolves into a literal street brawl that feels wildly out of place in a supposed "prestige" drama.

---

### *Max Payne*: Style Over Substance and Sanitized Noir

Where *Pride and Glory* takes itself too seriously, *Max Payne* fails by not taking its core material seriously enough. Based on Remedy Entertainment’s acclaimed 2001 video game, the film follows Cold Case detective Max Payne (Mark Wahlberg), whose obsession with solving his wife and child’s murder leads him into a underworld conspiracy involving a high-tech designer drug ("Aesir"), corporate espionage, and corrupt superiors.

#### The Good
Visually, *Max Payne* is occasionally striking. Director John Moore uses a desaturated, snow-drenched color palette interrupted by stark, fiery hues. The visual representation of the drug’s hallucinatory side effects—hallmark winged Valkyries hovering over a freezing New York skyline—provides a unique, comic-book-gothic aesthetic that separates it from standard police procedurals.

#### Where It Fails
The film fundamentally misunderstands both neo-noir and its own source material. The original *Max Payne* game was a brilliant love letter to hardboiled detective fiction, graphic novels, and Hong Kong action cinema, elevated by dark, poetic internal monologues. The film adaptation, burdened by a PG-13 rating, neuters the visceral violence that defined the game’s "bullet-time" identity. 

Wahlberg gives a flat, somnambulistic performance, mistaking tragic grief for sullen boredom. Furthermore, the film commits the cardinal sin of the corrupt cop subgenre: it converts a story of institutional rot and personal grief into a generic sci-fi corporate conspiracy. The corruption isn't a commentary on power, law, or morality—it is simply a plot point orchestrated by a mustache-twirling executive (Ludacris’s character notwithstanding) and a dirty ex-partner (Beau Bridges).

---

### Comparative Analysis: Two Sides of the Same Broken Coin

Comparing the two films reveals a stark contrast in execution, but an identical narrative dead end:

| Feature | *Pride and Glory* | *Max Payne* |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Approach to Genre** | Ultra-traditional, melodramatic police procedural. | Stylized neo-noir, tech-thriller/action hybrid. |
| **Nature of Corruption** | Institutional, familial, protectionist ("The Blue Wall"). | Corporate, conspiratorial, tied to a rogue drug plot. |
| **Tone** | Relentlessly bleak, hyper-serious. | Glossy, gothic, stylized escapism. |
| **Core Flaw** | Over-reliance on exhausted, heavy-handed tropes. | Complete lack of narrative weight and toothless action. |

*Pride and Glory* tries to elevate its familiar plot with heavy-handed emotional drama, but collapses under the weight of its own clichés. *Max Payne* tries to hide its empty narrative beneath CGI visual effects and moody cinematography, but ends up pleasing neither video game fans nor moviegoers. 

---

### Why Modern Hollywood Struggles with the Corrupt Cop Genre

The simultaneous failure of these two 2008 films highlights a broader, persistent crisis in Hollywood: **the inability to innovate within police-focused crime stories.** There are three main reasons for this ongoing struggle:

#### 1. The "Bad Apple" Fallacy vs. Systemic Reality
Mainstream studio filmmaking historically prefers the "Bad Apple" narrative: a system is fundamentally good, but has been infected by a few rogue individuals who must be purged by an honest hero (Ray Tierney or Max Payne). However, modern audiences are increasingly aware that police corruption is often systemic, procedural, and bureaucratic, rather than the work of isolated comic-book villains. When Hollywood reduces corruption to "a dirty cop threatening a baby" or "a evil corporation selling combat drugs," it feels disingenuous, dated, and intellectually lazy. 

#### 2. The Dominance of Long-Form Television
The corrupt cop genre requires time, room to breathe, and moral gray areas—things television learned to do infinitely better than two-hour feature films. Shows like *The Wire*, *The Shield*, and later *Line of Duty* and *We Own This City* thoroughly dismantled the police drama. They rendered films like *Pride and Glory* obsolete by showing the intricate, mundane, and structural realities of institutional decay. A two-hour movie can no longer compete with 10 hours of nuanced character development without resorting to rushed clichés.

#### 3. Fear of True Moral Ambiguity
Modern studio films rarely want their protagonists to be genuinely tarnished. In classic 1970s neo-noirs, or even 2001's *Training Day*, the line between the "good guys" and "bad guys" was thoroughly blurred. In both *Max Payne* and *Pride and Glory*, the protagonists remain frustratingly saintly. Ray Tierney and Max Payne are noble, brooding stoics who never actually participate in the corruption; they merely react to it. By keeping the hero’s hands entirely clean, the films rob the audience of genuine tension and moral conflict.

### Conclusion

*Pride and Glory* and *Max Payne* stand as twin monuments to a genre in creative paralysis. One represents Hollywood looking backward, desperately re-reading old pages from the 1970s gritty-cop playbook without understanding what made them work. The other represents Hollywood looking forward, trying to sanitize and stylize crime fiction into a marketable PG-13 franchise. 

Until cinema is willing to embrace genuine moral grayness, abandon tired family-drama tropes, and confront the complex, institutional nature of corruption rather than masking it behind cartoon villains or bullet-time CGI, the corrupt cop genre will continue to chase its own tail.
